chapters.n: Jonah was a real prophet from Galilee who served during the reign of Jeroboam II (around 790–750 BC). The Lord now gives him an unusual assignment.

f.g: His name means “dove.”

chapters.n: God sends Jonah to Nineveh, a great city of Assyria — Israel’s brutal enemy — to warn it. God cares even about Israel’s enemies.

f.g: A major city, later the capital, of the Assyrian Empire, on the Tigris River in modern Iraq.

f.w: their wickedness is come up before me

chapters.n: Jonah runs the opposite direction — west toward Tarshish, perhaps in Spain, the far edge of the known world. Notice he keeps going “down”: down to Joppa, down into the ship.

f.g: A distant port, probably in Spain — about as far from Nineveh as one could go.
A port on Israel’s Mediterranean coast; modern Jaffa, near Tel Aviv.

f.w: from the presence of the LORD

chapters.n: The Lord hurls a great wind onto the sea. The storm is so violent that the ship is about to break apart. You cannot outrun God.

f.w: the LORD sent out a great wind
f.g: Literally “hurled” a wind — the same verb used later when the sailors hurl cargo and Jonah overboard.

chapters.n: The pagan sailors pray desperately, each to his own god, and throw cargo overboard. Meanwhile Jonah has gone down into the ship’s hold and is sound asleep.

f.w: cried every man unto his god
f.g: The crew came from many nations and religions.
A deep sleep — the same word used for Adam’s sleep in Genesis 2:21.

chapters.n: The captain wakes Jonah: “How can you sleep? Get up and pray to your God! Maybe He will save us.” A pagan has to urge the prophet to pray.
The sailors cast lots to find out who is to blame, and the lot falls on Jonah. The Lord directs even this.
They pepper Jonah with questions: What do you do? Where are you from? What people are you?

f.g: Business or mission — ironically, Jonah is fleeing his.

chapters.n: Jonah declares he is a Hebrew who worships the Lord, Creator of sea and land. The irony: he claims to fear the God he is running from — the very God who made the sea he is sailing on.

f.g: To fear means to revere or worship.

chapters.n: Now the sailors are terrified. Jonah had told them he was fleeing from the Lord, and they realize how serious that is.
With the storm worsening, they ask Jonah what they should do to calm the sea.

f.g: Was growing more and more stormy.

chapters.n: Jonah tells them to throw him overboard. He accepts responsibility — though he would still rather die than go to Nineveh.

f.g: Because of me.

chapters.n: The kind-hearted sailors try hard to row back to shore rather than sacrifice Jonah, but the sea grows even wilder.

f.g: Literally “dug” — rowed with all their strength.

chapters.n: Now the sailors pray to Jonah’s God, the Lord, asking not to be held guilty for his death. These foreigners show more reverence than the prophet.
They throw Jonah into the sea, and it immediately becomes calm.

f.w: the sea ceased from her raging

chapters.n: The sailors now fear the Lord deeply, offer sacrifice, and make vows. Even Jonah’s disobedience led others to God.

f.g: Promises to God, often to offer sacrifices later.

chapters.n: God “prepared” a great fish to swallow Jonah — not to punish but to rescue him. Jesus cited Jonah’s three days in the fish as a sign of His own death and resurrection.

f.g: The Hebrew says “great fish,” not specifically a whale; Matthew’s Greek uses a word for “sea monster.”

chapters.n: From inside the fish, Jonah finally prays. Note “his God” — Jonah turns back to the God he tried to escape.
Jonah’s prayer is a psalm of thanksgiving. Even from what felt like the depths of death, he called and God heard him.

f.g: Hebrew Sheol — the realm of the dead; Jonah felt as good as dead.

f.w: I cried by reason of mine affliction unto the LORD, and he heard me

chapters.n: Jonah recognizes God’s hand: though the sailors threw him, it was the Lord who cast him into the deep. Waves and currents swept over him.

f.w: all thy billows and thy waves passed over me

chapters.n: Feeling banished from God’s presence, Jonah still resolves to look toward the temple — a sign of renewed faith.

f.w: I am cast out of thy sight

chapters.n: The water rose to his throat, the deep surrounded him, and seaweed wrapped around his head — a vivid picture of drowning.

f.g: Up to the neck or throat — to the point of death.

chapters.n: He sank to the roots of the mountains, locked in as if by the bars of death’s prison — yet God brought him up from the pit. The low point becomes a turning point.

f.g: The underworld pictured as a city with gates barred shut.
The pit, the grave.

chapters.n: When his life was ebbing away, Jonah remembered the Lord, and his prayer reached God’s holy temple.

f.w: When my soul fainted within me I remembered the LORD

chapters.n: Those who cling to worthless idols abandon the loyal love God offers them. Ironically, the idol-worshiping sailors had just turned to God.

f.g: Worthless idols; empty things.
Give up the steadfast love (Hebrew ḥesed) that could be theirs.

chapters.n: Jonah vows to give thanks and keep his promises. “Salvation is of the Lord” — the theme of the whole book.

f.w: I will pay that that I have vowed

chapters.n: The Lord speaks, and the fish spits Jonah out onto dry land. Even the creatures obey God more readily than His prophet had.

f.g: Cast out — an earthy, almost comic picture.

chapters.n: God gives Jonah a second chance, with the same call. The Lord is patient with His servants.

f.g: A comforting reminder that God offers second chances.

chapters.n: “Go to Nineveh and preach what I tell you.” This time Jonah must deliver God’s message, not his own.

f.w: the preaching that I bid thee

chapters.n: This time Jonah obeys. Nineveh was so large that it took three days to visit or cross the whole area.

f.g: May describe the city with its suburbs, or the time to make a full round of visits.

chapters.n: After a day’s walk into the city, Jonah announces: “Forty days, and Nineveh will be overthrown.” In Hebrew it is only five words — a short, bare sermon.

f.g: Forty is often a period of testing or preparation in scripture.
Hebrew haphak — the word used of Sodom’s overthrow; it can also mean “turned around,” which is what happened through repentance.

chapters.n: Amazingly, the Ninevites believe God. Everyone, from greatest to least, fasts and wears sackcloth. Jesus later held them up as an example of repentance.

f.w: the people of Nineveh believed God

f.g: Rough cloth worn in mourning and repentance.

chapters.n: The king himself steps down from his throne, removes his royal robe, and sits in ashes in humility.
The king decrees a total fast — even the animals may not eat or drink.

f.g: Including animals in mourning rituals was a known custom in the ancient world.

chapters.n: Everyone must cry mightily to God and turn from evil and violence. True repentance means changing behavior, not just rituals.

f.w: turn every one from his evil way

f.g: Assyria was notorious for cruelty in war.

chapters.n: “Who knows? Maybe God will relent and we won’t perish.” They hope in God’s mercy without presuming on it.
God sees their changed actions and relents from the disaster He had announced. His warnings are invitations; repentance changes outcomes.

f.g: Changed His mind about the disaster — not that God had done wrong.

chapters.n: Instead of rejoicing, Jonah is furious that God spared Nineveh. The most successful preacher in the Bible is upset by his success.

f.g: Literally “it was evil to Jonah, a great evil” — a play on the “evil” God had just withheld.

chapters.n: Jonah finally reveals why he ran: he knew God was gracious and merciful and would forgive the Ninevites. He quotes God’s own description of Himself — as a complaint!

f.w: a gracious God, and merciful, slow to anger

chapters.n: Jonah asks God to take his life, echoing Elijah’s despair under the juniper tree, but for a far less worthy reason.

f.w: it is better for me to die than to live

chapters.n: God responds gently with a question: “Is it right for you to be angry?” Like a patient teacher, He invites Jonah to examine his heart.

f.w: Doest thou well to be angry?

chapters.n: Jonah leaves, builds a shelter east of the city, and waits to see whether Nineveh will be destroyed after all.

f.g: A simple hut made of branches.

chapters.n: God makes a leafy plant grow quickly over Jonah to shade him. Jonah is very happy about the plant — the only time the book says he is glad.

f.g: Hebrew qiqayon — probably the castor-oil plant, a fast-growing shrub with broad leaves.
Appointed — the same verb used for the fish (1:17), the worm, and the wind.

chapters.n: Next morning God sends a worm to attack the plant, and it withers.

f.g: A grub or caterpillar.

chapters.n: Then God sends a scorching east wind. With the sun beating on his head, Jonah grows faint and again wishes to die.

f.g: A hot desert wind, sometimes called a sirocco.

chapters.n: God asks again: “Is it right to be angry about the plant?” Jonah snaps back, “Yes, angry enough to die!”

f.g: Angry enough to die — a stubborn, sulking reply.

chapters.n: The Lord draws the lesson: you cared about a plant you didn’t plant or tend, which lived only a night.

f.w: Thou hast had pity on the gourd
f.g: Jonah’s concern was really for his own comfort.

chapters.n: Shouldn’t I care about Nineveh, with more than 120,000 people who don’t know right from left — and many animals? The book ends with God’s question hanging, inviting every reader to share God’s compassion for all people.

f.g: A score is 20; sixscore thousand is 120,000.

f.w: cannot discern between their right hand and their left hand
f.g: Morally or spiritually untaught — or possibly small children.
